subtopics.title: Greenland's Status within Denmark, NATO and the EU
subtopics.summary: Greenland is one of Denmark's two autonomous territories and became a Danish colony after Hans Egede's expedition arrived in 1721. It became a self-governing territory in 1979 and has held the right to declare independence through a referendum since 2009. Through Denmark it is part of NATO, while it is associated with the EU as one of the EU Overseas Countries and Territories.
facts: Greenland is the world's largest island and one of Denmark's two autonomous territories
The other autonomous territory of Denmark is the Faroe Islands
Greenland became a Danish colony in the early 18th century after Hans Egede's expedition arrived in 1721
Greenland became a self-governing territory in 1979
Since 2009 Greenland has had the right to declare independence through a referendum
Greenland is part of NATO by default because Denmark is a NATO member
Greenland is not an EU member state but is associated with the EU as an Overseas Country and Territory
Greenlanders are considered to be EU citizens
Greenland joined the European Community with Denmark in 1973 and left it in 1985

subtopics.title: US Strategic and Military Ties with Greenland
subtopics.summary: The United States seized temporary control of Greenland during the Second World War to stop Nazi Germany from exploiting the Danish colony. It proposed a $100 million purchase offer to Denmark in 1946 and formalised American military access through a 1951 defence agreement. Today the US maintains Pituffik Space Base, which helps monitor potential missile threats.

subtopics.title: Critical Minerals and Emerging Arctic Shipping Routes
subtopics.summary: Greenland has large untapped reserves of rare earth elements, which are crucial for semiconductors, renewable energy and defence systems. These reserves offer the West an alternative supply chain to China-dominated rare earth markets. Melting Arctic ice is opening new maritime corridors, such as the Transpolar Sea Route, that could shorten Atlantic-Pacific travel and bypass the Panama and Suez Canals.

subtopics.title: Great Power Competition and the EU Anti-Coercion Instrument
subtopics.summary: China labels itself a Near-Arctic State and invests in Arctic research, while Russia has heavily militarised its Arctic coastline and the US views Greenland as central to countering both. Denmark's firm stance highlights the tension between territorial sovereignty and the strategic ambitions of major powers. The EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument, nicknamed the Trade Bazooka, is primarily a deterrent tool against economic coercion.

quizzes.title: Greenland's Status: Practice Set
quizzes.passage: Greenland is the world's largest island and forms one of Denmark's two autonomous territories, the other being the Faroe Islands. Its relationship with Denmark has a long history. The island became a Danish colony in the early eighteenth century, after an expedition led by the Danish-Norwegian missionary Hans Egede arrived in 1721. It became a self-governing territory in 1979, and since 2009 it has held the right to declare independence through a referendum. The island's status is now at the centre of a fresh dispute. Denmark's Prime Minister, Mette Frederiksen, has rejected United States claims on Greenland and reaffirmed Danish sovereignty over the Arctic territory. Greenland's place in wider alliances is shaped by Denmark's membership of NATO. Since Denmark is part of the alliance, Greenland is by default part of it as well. Greenland is not a member state of the European Union, but it is associated with the Union as one of the EU Overseas Countries and Territories. As a result, Greenlanders are considered to be EU citizens. Together, its autonomy, its right to independence and its alliance links explain why the island matters to Denmark, Europe and the United States.

Assertion (A): Greenland gives the North Atlantic a strategic role in monitoring naval movements.
Reason (R): The GIUK Gap is named after Greenland, Ireland and the United Kingdom.

questions.explanation: The GIUK Gap stands for Greenland, Iceland and United Kingdom, not Ireland, and it is a key chokepoint for monitoring naval movements.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Pituffik Space Base   ->   C. Formerly known as Thule Air Base
II. US proposal of 1946   ->   D. Offer of $100 million to Denmark for outright purchase
III. 1951 agreement   ->   A. US-Denmark Defence Agreement on military access
IV. Rare earth elements   ->   B. Crucial for semiconductors, renewable energy and defence systems
questions.explanation: Pituffik was formerly Thule Air Base, the 1946 proposal was a $100 million purchase offer, the 1951 agreement covered military access, and rare earths are crucial for semiconductors and defence systems.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Russia has heavily militarised the Arctic coastline.
II. China labels itself a Near-Arctic State.
III. The United States proposed to buy Greenland from Denmark in 1951.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while the US purchase proposal was made in 1946, not 1951.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Greenland and the EU:
I. Greenland joined the European Community together with Denmark in 1973 but left in 1985.
II. The Anti-Coercion Instrument was designed mainly as a tool for direct military retaliation.
III. The Transpolar Sea Route is one of the emerging Arctic shipping routes linked to melting ice.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement I and III are correct, while the Anti-Coercion Instrument is primarily a deterrent tool rather than a military one.

questions.q: What name does the booklet give to the EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument?
questions.explanation: The booklet calls the Anti-Coercion Instrument the 'Trade Bazooka'.

questions.q: Which body takes decisions to invite a country to join NATO?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the North Atlantic Council, NATO's principal political decision-making body, takes any decision to invite a country to join.

questions.q:
Statement I: Under Article 5, an armed attack on one NATO Ally is treated as an attack on all members.
Statement II: NATO was created by 12 countries on 4 April 1949.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Both statements appear in the booklet's NATO section: the Article 5 provision and the 1949 founding by 12 countries.

quizzes.title: Minerals and Arctic Routes: Typed Answers
quizzes.passage: Climate change is reshaping the Arctic. Melting sea ice is opening new maritime corridors through waters that were once difficult to navigate. Shipping along these corridors could shorten travel times between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, while lowering fuel and shipping costs. The new routes could also allow ships to avoid some of the chokepoints that currently shape global trade. Control over these sea lanes is expected to influence future trade flows and the projection of naval power. Greenland's own resources add to the region's importance. The island holds mineral wealth that is vital for semiconductors, renewable energy equipment and defence systems. Many Western economies see new sources of these minerals as a way to diversify supply chains that are heavily concentrated elsewhere. This push forms part of a wider effort to decouple sensitive economic sectors from rival suppliers. Outside powers are also investing in Arctic research and infrastructure, which signals long-term interest in the region. Taken together, the changing Arctic is becoming a centre of economic and strategic competition, and the outcome will shape which countries gain leverage over future trade.
